Senses.Explanation: Hanshan is the pre-Zen figure whom the records pair with Shide and Fenggan. The string is attested, but that total mixes the person with ordinary and place-name uses. The Continued Record preserves Shishuang Qingzhu's inherited list—rest, cease, let one thought last ten thousand years, go like cold ashes and dead wood—inside a sermon where Yunfeng quotes it, identifies it as an old master's view, and criticizes a one-sided reading by supplying the contrary, noisy sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease." Chenghui Xianxu says that downward discussion would make dead wood flower and cold ashes burst into flame. Lianfeng sets yesterday's ground-covering cold ashes against today's sky-filling news of spring. The ordinary ash, the criticized stillness formula, and the rekindling or seasonal reversals are one material image under different predicates, not different lexical things.

Senses.Explanation: A cold stove is an unlit or spent hearth that Chan poems and addresses make the site of an unexpected coal, spark, or winter gathering. Juelang Daosheng says Danxia's burning of a wooden Buddha merely adds charcoal to a cold stove. Another winter-solstice address announces a single spark bursting from one and then points to the whisk as what has burst forth. Seasonal poems retain the concrete stove beside cold, clothing, and year-end gathering. Those literal predicates control the image even where the hall address turns it into a surprise.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary usage, ‘capture and release’ is a commander’s battlefield tactic: take the opponent, then let him go at will. Chan speakers bend that command pair toward control of an encounter, repeatedly coordinating it with rolling out and folding up or killing and giving life. That command register is the word's Zen bend. Literally, 'capture and release': 'capture' (擒) paired with 'let loose or release' (縱). The compound is repeatedly attested representing 81 works. Its most frequent fixed relations are 'capture and release, kill and bring to life' (擒縱殺活, 20 occurrences) and 'roll out and fold up, capture and release' (卷舒擒縱, recurrent attestations representing 10 works). Yuanwu also records the reversed framing 'release and gather, capture and release' (放收擒縱) and says, 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me' (擒縱非他。卷舒在我). In an assembly address he writes that only afterward does one 'release and gather, capture and release, and obtain great freedom' (放收擒縱得大解脫). Another address says, 'within killing there is bringing to life, capturing and releasing humans and gods; within bringing to life there is killing, weighing buddhas and ancestors' (殺中有活擒縱人天。活中有殺權衡佛祖). His Essentials states: 'able to capture and release, skilled in killing and bringing to life—great teachers do not fail to use these' (能擒縱，善殺活，得大解脫，知識無不用之). Later commemorative prose similarly says 'capture and release, killing and bringing to life, are all complete' (擒縱殺活皆全). The corpus thus deploys the pair as the cited speaker's coordinated command of the encounter, commonly placed in four-part action strings.

Senses.Explanation: The blade's exposed sharpness (鋒鋩) is the edge or point by which it can wound. Chan records make exposure itself the test: monks ask how to win without displaying the edge, masters warn against touching or avoiding it, and death verses say that not even a drop of it should be conceded. The word therefore joins sharp effectiveness to whether that effectiveness leaves a visible trace; it is not merely a decorative sword part.
